item.title: Trump Calls Former Lawyer’s $50 Million Deal ‘Obnoxious and Outrageous’
item.description:
President Trump on Saturday strongly criticized his former lawyer, Alina Habba Mildon, saying it was “totally obnoxious and outrageous” for her to enter into a $50 million deal for work with a billionaire Venezuelan family seeking a pardon from the president.

Mrs. Mildon, while working as a senior adviser at the Justice Department, signed on last year as an extraordinarily well-compensated general counsel for a company started by the daughter of Julio Herrera Velutini, who was granted the pardon by Mr. Trump weeks later.

At a Halloween party on Saturday at his Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Fla., Mr. Trump tore into Mrs. Mildon when asked about the contract, calling it “not acceptable.”

“I thought it was terrible,” he told reporters. “I told her, and I said, ‘I don’t want her paid.’ I thought we had somebody speak to the people that did it, and she used her relationship to do that. And it was far too much.”

Mrs. Mildon, who served as a personal lawyer to Mr. Trump and then briefly as the U.S. attorney in New Jersey, signed a four-year contract to represent the family. It is unclear if the deal can be terminated early.

When Mr. Trump first learned about Mrs. Mildon’s arrangement from an article in The New York Times, he erupted and told aides and allies that Mrs. Mildon should donate a portion of the money to his future presidential library or another Trump-related entity.

Mr. Trump said Saturday that he did not necessarily expect Mrs. Mildon to make a donation to the library, but suggested that someone should.

“I expect maybe the people,” he said of the Herrera family. “I don’t know if anybody wants to make it. But it’s unacceptable what she did.”

The contract calls for the Herrera family to pay Mrs. Mildon $10 million a year for four years, along with a variety of bonuses. In total, she was guaranteed more than $50 million, according to interviews and documents obtained by The Times.

Mrs. Mildon formally began her work for the family on Jan. 1. Weeks later, Mr. Trump granted Mr. Herrera a full and unconditional pardon for a misdemeanor campaign finance violation. Mr. Herrera had faced felony bribery charges but struck an unusually lenient plea deal in 2025. Mrs. Mildon previously said she played no role in Mr. Herrera’s pardon.

She did not respond to a request for comment about Mr. Trump’s criticism on Saturday.

item.title: ‘I Came as Donald Trump’: The President Hosts a Luxury Halloween at Mar-a-Lago
item.description:
There were cheetah and zebra stripes on the walls and tables. Women wore sequined leotards and elaborate headdresses, and one couple flocked around in bright-feathered costumes of jungle birds. Then President Trump arrived.

“I came as Donald Trump,” he said, outfitted in his standard red tie and navy suit. “I didn’t have time to get — people spent a lot of time and money. Rich people. They spent nine hours getting ready. I had 10 minutes, so I came as Donald Trump.”

Such was the scene Saturday night, when hundreds gathered in the ballroom at Mar-a-Lago to celebrate Halloween with the president. The theme was the jungle, if an opulent one.

There was Alaskan king crab and a caviar bar. There were bongo drums and puppets. Attendees posted photos on social media that showed a pen at the club with a zebra and a miniature pony. Nothing too scary.

Much more frightening for Republicans is the political environment across the country. And yet even as they brace for potential losses on Tuesday, Mr. Trump, whose approval rating is near historic lows, was thrilled to be entertaining.

“Look at all my rich members,” he told reporters. “They spent all day getting ready. Look at these guys.”

He added: “These are the biggest guys on Wall Street.”

It was a striking tone, with polls showing voters souring even more on Mr. Trump’s handling of the economy. One recent one from The New York Times and Siena University found that a majority of voters blame Mr. Trump for the decline: 69 percent disapprove of his handling of the cost of living, 65 percent disapprove of the war in Iran, and nearly 75 percent disapprove of the high price of gas and diesel.

But for Mr. Trump, Mar-a-Lago is always a stage for his brand of gilded festivity.

There was Speaker Mike Johnson and Sergio Gor, the U.S. ambassador to India, in the cordoned-off section of the ballroom. Attorney General Todd Blanche, who traveled with Mr. Trump on Air Force One on Friday, told reporters that he planned to wear an astronaut suit to the party. Vice President JD Vance was back in Washington, dressed as Albus Dumbledore as part of a family Harry Potter set of costumes.

Mr. Trump entered the ballroom to fanfare and gabbed with reporters on the dance floor before mingling with his “rich friends,” as he kept calling them. He castigated Alina Habba Mildon, his former personal lawyer, over a $50 million deal she secured for work with a billionaire Venezuelan family seeking a pardon from the president. He weighed in on the feud between Representative Haley Stevens of Michigan and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for Senate.

And he addressed, for the first time, a report in The New York Times that Jensen Huang, the chief executive of Nvidia and an adviser to Mr. Trump, was the target of a Chinese spy plot.

“I have a lot of respect for him. I like him. We hope everything’s OK,” he said. “We’ll check it out. We’re going to check it out very closely.”

When asked if Mr. Huang would stay on as a member of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, Mr. Trump said he “would like to say yes.”

“I mean, unless we find out something to the contrary,” he said. “I’ve always found Jensen Huang to be very above board. But you know, you’re dealing in a very complex issue, I will say.”

The Halloween party landed at a complicated moment for the president. He has spent much of the last month crisscrossing the country holding rallies for Republican candidates, many of them even or lagging in the polls. Some have sought to distance themselves from the president’s unpopular policies.

Mr. Trump was originally scheduled to travel to Kansas on Saturday for a rally, then to Iowa on Sunday. But on Thursday, both were canceled. A day later, after the president chewed out a reporter for asking why the first rally was canceled, the events were back on, but rescheduled as a double-header on Sunday.

Before the Halloween bash, Mr. Trump spent much of the day at his golf course in West Palm Beach, and participating in virtual rallies for Republican candidates.

“I feel very good,” the president told reporters, with the feathered guests gawking at him. “I mean, I feel like we’re doing well. The country has never done better.”

item.title: Ocasio-Cortez Has Evolved. She Wants the Left to Evolve, Too.
item.description:
Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has done a lot of growing up in the eight years since a stunning upset catapulted her from anonymous 20-something insurgent to establishment-busting avatar of American progressivism. She is pursuing alliances across the political spectrum rather than flaming other Democrats, betting that bridge-building is a better way to expand her movement.

She would like to see the left grow up, too.

In private discussions, she has urged fellow democratic socialists to foster a “culture of welcoming” rather than of “intimidation,” mindful that even she has sometimes failed their purity-minded litmus tests on issues like the war in Gaza.

She has called for “really big carrots” to attract new allies, talking up donations to colleagues in competitive House districts who take risky progressive stances.

And as she zigzags the country campaigning for some of the most liberal new voices in politics, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has taken pains to present herself as a kind of friendly neighborhood lefty: She will preach warmly to the unconverted, she suggests, whether they like it or not.

“I’ve had people say, ‘Well, we don’t want you at our luncheon’ or ‘We don’t want you around here,’” she told voters in Portland, Maine, while sharing a stage with Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate candidate. “And I’ll say, ‘That’s fine. I’m not going to stop trying to be your friend.’”

In public and private remarks, meetings with lawmakers and appearances with midterm candidates inside and outside the socialist ranks, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, 37, has begun sketching her preferred vision for the left’s next phase. She hopes to nudge the rambunctious coalition in a bigger-tent direction that mirrors her own path in Congress and stands to benefit both its collective agenda and her own potential ambitions.

She has repeatedly emphasized that she did not grow up in “a leftist household” (or, occasionally, a “militant leftist family”) that busied itself with high-minded political theory, positioning herself as an authentic champion of the working class who scrubbed toilets in her youth with her mother.

As she weighs runs for the presidency or the Senate in two years, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez hopes to establish herself as broadly palatable to Democrats — recently joking (but maybe also not entirely) that “Woke 1 was crazy” — without sounding too much like everyone else.

“There are more working people in this country than there are billionaires,” she told supporters of Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, last month inside a high school auditorium in Detroit, where students, exuberant grandparents and a man in an “ACTIVISTS NEVER RETIRE” shirt creaked in wooden seats. “There are more single moms. There are more working dads.”

The flourish registered, almost, as the founding sensibility of a campaign in waiting, one that might evoke and expand upon the nation’s two most electric political movements of the left in this century: the people-over-profits populism of Bernie Sanders and the more-unites-than-divides-us appeals of Barack Obama.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez appears to believe that her base is ready to hear both of those messages at once.

“A.O.C.’s possibility and challenge really exemplify that of the larger socialist movement,” said Daniel Denvir, a D.S.A. member who hosts a popular podcast for Jacobin, the socialist magazine. “She both needs to fire up and consolidate her support on the socialist left while also appealing to a broader array of liberal voters. And from nearly the beginning, there were people on the left who were in a hurry to condemn her as a sellout for no real reason.”

That posture has not always endeared the left to the rest of the political world. Despite breakthroughs in places like New York City and Providence, R.I., socialism is viewed negatively by roughly half of likely American voters, according to a recent poll conducted by The New York Times and Siena University, while 31 percent view it favorably.

Ahead of Tuesday’s elections, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez seems determined to demonstrate that her reach can be wider.

She has conferred with Black civil rights leaders and “Make America Healthy Again” activists. She has boosted Democrats in red states and directed money to the political operations of non-firebrands like Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor. She has toured the Deep South and upstate New York, where she pandered without apology in a Buffalo Bills sweatshirt.

And she has campaigned especially aggressively in Michigan, where the Senate race will stand as a meaningful test of how her politics might resonate in a presidential swing state.

“She has grown,” said Representative Nydia Velázquez of New York, an early Washington mentor with whom Ms. Ocasio-Cortez remains close. “D.S.A. needs to learn something from her.”

Eight and a half years ago, the D.S.A. remained a fringe actor in Democratic politics — with some 35,000 members, less than a third of the current tally — and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez betrayed little interest in becoming its public face.

While the group endorsed her, it was seen as a junior partner in her 2018 primary success. In interviews back then, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was reluctant to box herself in. She called democratic socialism “part of what I am” but “not all of what I am,” noting (presciently) that “plenty of socialists would say I’m not a socialist.”

“I don’t read a book and then decide what I am,” she told Hot 97 that July, saying that she cared more about policies like “Medicare for all” and tuition-free college than political labels. “If that makes me a socialist, then all right, well, I guess I’m a socialist. I guess I’m a democratic socialist.”

At the same time, two powerful forces with a keen interest in her rise — conservative media outlets hoping to elevate her as a far-left boogeywoman and socialist organizers eager to claim her as their own — were repeating the affiliation often enough for it to congeal into canon: A.O.C. and D.S.A., D.S.A. and A.O.C.

“I don’t think she realized that the democratic socialist label would become such an all-encompassing label that would be so attached to her,” said Bhaskar Sunkara, the president of The Nation magazine and a longtime D.S.A. member. “All the sudden she’s being asked to defend and be connected to a platform that I’m not sure she ever fully agreed with.”

Whatever the label, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez established herself quickly as one of the most left-wing members of Congress. She pushed the “Green New Deal.” She irritated Nancy Pelosi. She endorsed Mr. Sanders’s 2020 presidential campaign just after his heart attack, which for a time helped revive his bid.

That election year, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez emphasized positions she has been less inclined to highlight lately.

“Defunding police means defunding police,” she said that June, amid the wide-scale backlash to George Floyd’s killing. “It does not mean budget tricks or funny math.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has not clarified if this stance was part of the “Woke 1” craziness she cited, borrowing the phrase from a New York City councilman, Chi Ossé. When asked about the “Woke 1” comments in Nevada recently, she said she was referring not to policies but to her hope for a progressive movement “that is not rooted in judgment, castigation or being closed off.”

Supporters say she has begun modeling what a more accommodating left might look like, at no small cost to her credibility with some elements of the movement.

During Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s presidency, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez mostly determined, like Mr. Sanders, that working with the White House would be better for progressives than heckling from the sidelines.

After Mr. Biden’s disastrous 2024 debate performance, Ms. Ocasio-Cortez was one of the most prominent Democrats publicly arguing that he should remain on the ticket.

Perhaps her most striking turn came after Mr. Biden ended his campaign: She earned a prime convention slot, just before Hillary Clinton, to celebrate Vice President Kamala Harris.

To many within the D.S.A., Ms. Ocasio-Cortez sounded far more like a Democrat than a socialist, giving Ms. Harris political cover on a major vulnerability, the war in Gaza, with a line that continues to echo grimly in D.S.A. circles.

“She is working tirelessly to secure a cease-fire,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said of Ms. Harris, a remark that some pro-Palestinian activists continue to find offensively misleading.

By then, the national D.S.A., which is considered less pragmatic than its New York City chapter, had already loudly unendorsed Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, accusing her of “deep betrayal” and condemning her for not universally opposing funding for Israel, including its Iron Dome antimissile system, among other concerns. She has more recently sworn off sending any military aid to Israel.

To Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s defenders, maintaining credibility across the party was a requirement for an inside-outside strategy that was producing results. The Biden White House, no lefty radical’s idea of lefty radicals, had listened to their movement on issues like climate change and health care. Left-wing candidates were claiming more offices up and down the ballot, often with her help.

“My motivation is winning,” Ms. Ocasio-Cortez said flatly on the left-leaning podcast “The Majority Report” recently. “One thing that I don’t like to be is alone.”

On a private D.S.A. video call this year — a congressional re-endorsement forum during which members of the New York City chapter loaded the screen with emojis (thumbs up, thumbs down, eyeballs, Palestinian flags) as she spoke — Ms. Ocasio-Cortez had a request.

“I want to be judged as a human being and as a comrade,” she said, alluding to the prolific left-wing vitriol she had often read about herself as a doom-scrolling millennial. “I’m not asking for freedom from criticism. But I think what I am asking for is to be treated as a trusted person and friend.”

While the chapter voted overwhelmingly to re-endorse her, some who know Ms. Ocasio-Cortez see a cruel irony in how pockets of the left perceive her. She has helped elevate a new class of leaders, including Dr. El-Sayed (who is not in the D.S.A.) and Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York (who is) — and has occasionally suffered by comparison, in the eyes of some in the base.

Dr. El-Sayed, a student of the new attention economy whom Politico recently nicknamed “Hurricane Abdul,” has summoned a swaggering machismo that some supporters say is simply not an option for a woman in politics.

And Ms. Ocasio-Cortez is less instinctively tethered to the socialist project than Mr. Mamdani, who immersed himself in D.S.A. organizing well before his mayoral run. (Ms. Ocasio-Cortez, it emerged in August, had not even paid her membership dues for years. She quickly rejoined.)

While Mr. Mamdani has not universally pleased the left, it has long grated on some Ocasio-Cortez allies that the new mayor seems to be given more deference from more of the base than she was ever afforded.

Polling suggests that Mr. Mamdani is more popular.

“Imagine A.O.C. meeting with Bloomberg or some of the other corporate type guys,” Ms. Velázquez said, referring to Mr. Mamdani’s sessions with business leaders like Michael R. Bloomberg, the former New York mayor. “She would have been vilified. I think there is a different standard when it comes to her.”

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s own outreach has often taken different forms, hinting at her ambitions for the movement’s expansion — and at the “carrots” she can dangle. She recently poured $1 million into a political account for Dr. El-Sayed after sending $300,000 to help Democrats in New York.

She has advised activists to “grow movements instead of gate-keep them,” and cautioned supporters to consider the many areas where President Trump remains more popular than the Democratic Party and “work with that reality.”

Her wider endorsement slate has spanned from Tom Perriello, a former Virginia congressman running in a right-leaning House district, to Angie Nixon, a Florida state representative who is seeking to become the state’s first Black senator.

Ms. Nixon is among several Black leaders with whom Ms. Ocasio-Cortez has cultivated or deepened relationships ahead of the midterms — and ahead of 2028, when the Democratic presidential primary might well turn, as it often has, on which candidate performs best with Black voters.

“She’s really working to make sure the North and the South are connected,” said Justin Pearson, a state representative in Tennessee running for a House seat.

The Rev. Al Sharpton, who introduced Ms. Ocasio-Cortez in August at an anniversary rally for the March on Washington, said he had found her much more accessible than some of her ideological peers.

“She’s done something that a lot of D.S.A. people have not done,” Mr. Sharpton said, “which is reach out into communities that may not necessarily be supportive.”

For years, the left could be an almost consciously lonely place, exemplified by Mr. Sanders’s proudly iconoclastic monologues about millionaires and billionaires at the Capitol.

Ms. Ocasio-Cortez’s appearances with Mr. Sanders last year on their “Fighting Oligarchy” tour were rich with generation-bridging symbolism. But in some ways, the final days of her midterm travel have doubled as a next step: persuading audiences that there is nothing radical or doctrinaire about these beliefs.

“Good schools is not communism,” she said on Tuesday night at a “Boricuas for Angie” event with Ms. Nixon in Kissimmee, Fla. “Funded hospitals is not communism.”

A responsive government, she concluded, was neither extreme, nor outlandish, nor “out far left.”

And with that she introduced Ms. Nixon, who recently joined the D.S.A.

Benjamin Oreskes contributed reporting from New York City.

item.title: In L.A., a Stark Generational Divide May Determine the Mayor’s Race
item.description:
Saturday nights usually aren’t prime time for campaigning in Los Angeles elections. Still, there was Nithya Raman, stumping for mayor at a party at a Hollywood art gallery at 9 p.m. on a recent weekend.

Pink lights glowed. Pop tracks bumped. Gen Z influencers posed in a floral garland for Instagram and TikTok. If anyone in the house was a homeowner over 50, they didn’t look it.

“What is happening in Los Angeles is a generational election,” Ms. Raman, 45, said. In the audience, Sable Minx, a 28-year-old social media creator, applauded.

“I work, I would say, three jobs,” she said, “and I still can’t afford to, you know, live on my own, have my own space.” New leadership? That “resonated,” she said.

Though not with everyone.

The next morning Alton Reed, 80, headed out with his wife and a fistful of fliers to walk precincts for Mayor Karen Bass, the 73-year-old incumbent. “That’s the attitude of all young people, isn’t it,” he said, as he walked with a crowd of supporters. “‘Time for a change.’ Whether it’s warranted or not.”

That tension has underpinned the choice facing Los Angeles voters as they decide whether to keep their mayor or elect a new one. From policy proposals to celebrity endorsements, the most consistent subtext has been the age-based divide that has emerged in the nationally watched campaign.

Polls have consistently shown voters under 40 flocking to Ms. Raman, who has been backed by the democratic socialist movement that helped elect New York’s 35-year-old mayor, Zohran Mamdani. Voters over 65 have mostly stood by Ms. Bass, a former state lawmaker and member of Congress and a veteran Democrat.

The split echoes broader trends: Over the past two years, according to a New York Times/Siena University poll, young voters have swung dramatically to the view that the country is on the wrong track, a determination that, in this election at least, has yanked them leftward.

It has also prompted more young people to run for office. Future Caucus, a nonpartisan nonprofit that works with younger elected officials, reported this month that more than a third of this year’s congressional candidates were millennials or Gen Z, a new high for candidates under 45.

In Los Angeles, the margins have been stark, particularly among younger voters. In a survey conducted earlier this month for The Los Angeles Times by the Institute of Governmental Studies at the University of California, Berkeley, 69 percent of likely voters under 30 favored Ms. Raman, as did 74 percent of voters aged 30 to 39.

“Even more than with Mamdani, this is a campaign about generations,” said Dan Schnur, a former Republican political consultant who now teaches political communications at several universities in California.

On one side, he said, are longtime residents who respect the mayor’s deep experience and consider complaints about the current state of Los Angeles in the context of the chaotic city they once knew — a smog-clouded sprawl of racism, rioting, gang crime and police abuses that changed, in large measure, because of people like Ms. Bass. She’s an adult, they say, and this is no time to elect an untested leader, with two more years of the Trump administration and with the Summer Olympics coming in less than two years.

On the other side are waves of new voters who say they have been failed by the leadership of Ms. Bass and her generation. Many newcomers say the gritty city they’ve found doesn’t live up to its billing, and natives wonder what happened to the Southern California where single-family homes and single-occupancy cars were an affordable birthright.

“Think about what that generation has experienced — 9/11, the Great Recession, the #MeToo movement, Covid,” Mr. Schnur said of young voters. “It’s no wonder they’re searching for dramatic change.”

The schism is directly tied to affordability challenges like home prices and other markers of adulthood, which have increasingly moved out of reach for residents under 40. Young residents shoulder an average rent that, at $2,662, is more than 33 percent higher than the national average, according to Zillow. The average homeowner, according to an analysis of census data released last year, is older in Los Angeles than in any other big city in the nation — almost 55.

That calculus already has shifted the city’s conventional political wisdom. Since the early 1970s, when white, Black, Latino and Jewish liberals joined forces to elect the city’s first Black mayor, Tom Bradley, elections in the sprawling city have swung chiefly on the ability to assemble a coalition from socioeconomic and ethnic factions. This year, analysts say, there’s a new cohort.

“This is the first campaign I can recall where age was as significant a factor as racial demography,” said Jim Newton, a former head of the editorial page of The Los Angeles Times and lecturer on public policy at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Michael Rodriguez-Chen, 33, and his wife, Paula Rodriguez-Chen, 32, for example, say they will vote for Ms. Raman. Watching their 3-year-old son dart around a playground in the city’s Eagle Rock neighborhood, they ticked off an assortment of municipal complaints: deteriorating streets, sidewalks turned into mountain ranges by overgrown tree roots.

But what really stood out, Mr. Rodriguez-Chen said, was Ms. Raman’s promise to make housing more affordable by encouraging more apartment construction and establishing tenant protections.

The Rodriguez-Chens work from their two-bedroom, two-bathroom apartment not far from the playground. It’s a little cramped, but at $3,300 per month, it was a good deal. Similar places in their price range would have required them to choose: “Like, do we keep our couch or our table?” recalled Ms. Rodriguez-Chen wryly.

But how long will they stay there? The couple said they didn’t feel they had much choice.

“I don’t know if we’re able to currently move forward,” Mr. Rodriguez-Chen said.

That experience is a far cry from that of Inja Lee, 84, a retiree in the city’s Koreatown district who showed up with scores of Korean American seniors at a recent meet-and-greet with the mayor. Ms. Lee said she appreciated Ms. Bass’s efforts to address homelessness and public safety concerns.

Her experience in Los Angeles dates to the tumultuous 1990s, a decade convulsed by the Los Angeles riots, the Northridge earthquakes and the trial of O.J. Simpson. The proprietor of a greeting card store in nearby Burbank for several decades, she now lives in a Koreatown senior housing complex.

The mayor seemed to understand Los Angeles, she said. “She moved the homeless people to a good place,” Ms. Lee said. “She’s a nice lady. And we know her.”

That split screen extends in ways large and small across the two campaigns. Gen X and millennial stars like Natalie Portman and Poppy Liu dominate Ms. Raman’s list of celebrity supporters. Ms. Bass’s roster reads like a who’s who of silver Angelenos: Jane Fonda, Magic Johnson, Samuel L. Jackson.

Ms. Raman has support from the Los Angeles chapter of the Democratic Socialists of America and most of the transit enthusiasts and lobbies. Ms. Bass has the business establishment, most of the major City Hall unions, the police and every member of the City Council except for Ms. Raman.

Ms. Raman’s campaign has been heavily online, with social media posts featuring influencers and spoofs of microdramas. Ms. Bass’s supporters have papered the city with old-school handouts and door hangers. (The mayor, Mr. Schnur observed with a chuckle, “is running an almost perfect 20th-century campaign.”)

“I’m saddened by it,” Ms. Bass said of the generational divide, pointing to her years as a student activist, her work as a young physician assistant organizing against the 1980s crack epidemic and her mentorship of young Black and Latino leaders at the nonprofit she founded, Community Coalition. If re-elected, she said, her administration will give young people a bigger role.

“But I also understand it, because I was one of those young leaders once,” she said in an interview. “And I was very disgruntled and very dissatisfied and very angry at the status quo.”

The raw numbers would seem to favor Team Raman: almost 57 percent of the city’s electorate is under 50. But turnout is notoriously unpredictable among younger voters. As of Saturday, only 8 percent of Los Angeles voters under 35 had returned their ballots, compared with 31 percent of voters over 65, according to the California-based research firm Political Data Intelligence.

“Now, young people, historically, have not voted in municipal elections,” Ms. Raman called out to her supporters. “Are we going to make our voices heard this time?”

item.title: Threats, Gaffes and Men’s Posteriors: Trump’s Talk Gets Wilder
item.description:
As he opened his speech at a recent campaign rally in Greenville, N.C., President Trump told the story of the Willie Horton crime case that helped sink the presidential campaign of the Democrat Michael S. Dukakis in 1988.

And then, 30 minutes later, still speaking at the same rally to the same audience from the same lectern, Mr. Trump told the same Willie Horton story all over again, using some of the same language (and getting the facts wrong both times).

Mr. Trump, who last year became the oldest person ever inaugurated as president and turned 80 in June, has demonstrated physical stamina as he barnstorms the country in advance of midterm elections. But his performances on the road and at the White House this fall have produced many head-scratching moments that have revived questions about his age and stability.

He can be forgetful and repetitive. He is more long-winded, more profane and more absolutist than when he ran for president a decade ago. His rambling speeches seem even more garbled at times. He makes comments that leave people wondering what he is talking about or that sound like he is saying something he is not. And even for a president who has never fully observed the norms of the office, he seems more willing to say things no other president would say.

He declared that at an unfenced construction site “only a Hispanic could survive that fall.” He wants to ban immigrants from Norway “because I didn’t get the Nobel Prize.” He says “I don’t give a damn” if he is seen as caring more about oil company profits than struggling workers. He mispronounces the Strait of Hormuz as the “Hormone Strait.” He has told supporters to “cheat like hell” in the Nov. 3 elections. He says military leakers “should be shot.” And then there is his baffling fixation with admiring men’s posteriors.

Even Mr. Trump seems astonished at times by what comes out of his mouth — and by how much his supporters embrace him nonetheless. “I could say the stupidest things and you’d clap. ‘Oh, I love you so,’” he marveled at a recent rally in Clarksville, Tenn. “But we don’t say the stupidest things,” he quickly added. “We say things of common sense. We say things that make sense.”

For Mr. Trump, making sense often places second to having fun at rallies, and some outrageous remarks appear aimed at generating a laugh. His allies say too much is made of comments that are really just jokes. He has always been a provocative speaker, willing to outrage for the sake of outrage. Mr. Trump defends his stream-of-consciousness rambling as a “brilliant” speaking style that he calls “the weave.”

But the weave seems to be getting weavier. An A.I.-assisted New York Times review of Mr. Trump’s comments from speeches, rallies, social media, interviews and public meetings found significant changes since he began a run for president at age 69 in 2015, although not as much of a notable shift since 2024 when a similar review was conducted. Broadly speaking, the review concluded, Mr. Trump’s public communication is more vulgar, more uninhibited and less coherent than it was a decade ago.

“He’s saying so many stupid things, even for him, so many outrageous and aggressive things,” said former Representative Francis Rooney, a Republican from Florida. “This aggressive kind of attack language, that’s something I’ve never heard from a president.”

The White House denied that Mr. Trump has lost a step. Davis Ingle, a White House spokesman, hailed his “sharpness, unmatched energy, relentless work ethic and historic accessibility” and dismissed concerns about his provocative comments.

“The president doesn’t care about being politically correct, he cares about making America great again,” Mr. Ingle said. “The American people love how authentic, transparent and effective the president is.”

Measuring the effects of age can be difficult without a medical exam, although that has not stopped many physicians, political commentators and everyday Americans from drawing conclusions about Mr. Trump based on what they see on television.

The Times review from 2015 through Thursday found that the president in his second term has used 19 percent more all-or-nothing words like “always,” “never,” “everything” and “totally” at rallies than he did a decade ago and 5 percent more than in 2024, a sign of black-and-white thinking that experts say often accompanies advancing age or cognitive decline. He is cruder than he used to be, using nearly 15 swear words per 10,000 words compared with 14 two years ago and six a decade ago, a change consistent with age-related disinhibition.

The review, relying on an A.I.-assisted metric, found that he makes rambling or confusing digressions in his rallies and speeches two and a half times as often in his second term as in the 2016 campaign, although roughly the same as in 2024. His vocabulary remains about the same, as does the reading level of his speaking, which hovers between fourth and fifth grade. (The average modern president speaks at an eighth-grade level.)

Mr. Trump’s public schedule is thinner, down to 1.3 events per weekday versus 2.1 in the first term. But he is posting online an average of 21 times a day, up from 13 a day in 2016 although down from 34 a day two years ago. The night owl president has posted messages between midnight and 5 a.m. on 30 percent of his nights in his second term and has had 240 bursts of 10 or more posts an hour.

The president’s doctor has said that Mr. Trump is mentally sharp. In a three-page summary released in May, Dr. Sean P. Barbabella, the White House physician, noted that Mr. Trump had scored 30 out of 30 on the Montreal Cognitive Assessment. “Cognitive and physical performance are excellent,” he wrote.

The Montreal assessment is a quick test to screen for Alzheimer’s disease or other cognitive impairment and includes basic questions like identifying a lion, camel and rhinoceros; drawing a clock; repeating words or numbers in order; and naming as many words as possible in one minute that start with the letter F. “Nobody can do this,” Mr. Trump insisted a couple weeks ago, adding: “But I can. You know why? Because I’m a freaking genius!”

Mr. Trump appears sensitive to the perception that he is slipping, bringing up his cognitive tests without being asked at a half-dozen recent rallies. In Chillicothe, Ohio, on Wednesday night, he called himself “a very high-IQ person,” offered an extended description of the tests and compared his brainpower to that of former Presidents Barack Obama and Joseph R. Biden Jr.

“Don’t forget I’m the only president to pass without exception — I passed three cognitive tests,” he said. “I’m the only president that agreed to take them. And they’re hard, you know? Obama couldn’t have passed it. Biden we don’t even talk about.”

While Mr. Trump has been known to nod off during White House meetings, he draws energy from crowds when he is on the road. He speaks and speaks and speaks — twice as long as in 2016, according to the Times review, for an average of 85 minutes per rally compared with 42 minutes a decade ago.

He is profoundly and proudly undisciplined. He says things that are manifestly unhelpful to him. Even as many Americans are upset about the cost of filling their gas tank, he said in Perry, Ga., the other day that high oil prices were good because the fossil fuel industry was making hundreds of billions of dollars. Even as he said it, he acknowledged it would produce bad headlines. “I don’t give a damn,” he said. “I’m going to say it. We’re making a freaking fortune.”

He wanders from thought to thought, often without finishing a sentence, embedding one off-the-cuff story within another. In Pendleton, S.C., he started talking about transgender athletes, interrupted to tell a story about someone he met in Israel, referred to a poll without explaining its results and then riffed on climate change:

“You have a lot of records that are not exactly going to be shattered by women. They’re going to say, ‘Who the hell broke it?’ Or the swimmer who was a great swimmer, and then she looked to her left, she looked to her right, and she saw this massive human being next to her.

You’ve seen him — her on television. And she had to compete. And my wife said, ‘Please don’t tell those stories. They’re terrible stories to tell as president. Can you imagine George Washington telling these stories?’ No, because George Washington lived in sanity. He didn’t have men playing in women’s sports.

I promise you this. I didn’t know George Washington personally, but they did not have the mutilization of your children for transgender purposes. Do you think George ever had any of the things that we have to go through, Tim? I don’t think so.

Abraham Lincoln — I met a young man from Israel. I said, ‘Who’s your favorite president?’ He said, ‘Abraham Lincoln.’ I said, ‘Oh.’ I said, ‘That’s nice.’ We love Abraham Lincoln. But you’re going to see something later, because they have a poll — they took a poll recently. You’re going to see it. But I also declared a national emergency on energy and terminated the Green New Scam, one of the greatest hoaxes in the history of our country.”

Like many people in their ninth decade, he is prone to say things that seem inappropriate. His focus on the male anatomy, for instance, has become remarkably pronounced lately.

“I don’t do this with men very often,” Mr. Trump said at a rally with Senator Jon Husted, Republican of Ohio, on Oct. 12. “I started examining his body because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass.”

Five days later, he repeated his appreciation of Mr. Husted’s backside. “I examined his ass,” Mr. Trump said at a rally in Kentucky. “I never did that with, no, I never did that with a man before.” Three days later in North Carolina, he praised Mr. Husted’s derrière again. “His ass is, it’s like a pile of muscle,” he said. In Chillicothe, he did it again: “I started by looking at his ass, and it was strong as hell.”

Mr. Husted is not the only object of Mr. Trump’s manly approval. Among the others:

Senator Tim Scott, Republican of South Carolina: “As much as I can fall in love with a man, which isn’t that much, I fall in love with him, and his name happens to be Tim Scott.”

The spouse of Senator Darline Graham, the other South Carolina Republican: “He’s a good-looking husband.”

Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the health and human services secretary: “He’s got the body of a 30-year-old.”

Representative Mike Collins, Republican of Georgia: “Mike Collins is a good-looking man. And he’s all man.”

In Michigan on Sunday, Mr. Trump made a point of praising a woman’s backside for a change. “I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before — Nicki Minaj,” he told the crowd. “That’s hard to miss.”

Mr. Trump has always displayed fits of public anger in ways that other presidents have not. But he seems even more prone to pounce these days.

He snaps at reporters so often now that he barely waits for their questions before calling them “sick” and ordering, “Quiet!” When a reporter asked on Thursday if he was canceling a trip to Kansas because he was tired of traveling, Mr. Trump accosted his physical appearance. “You are disgusting! Put yourself in shape. You look like hell.”

His exhortations to supporters to vote have grown more vulgar and violent as well. “If you do that,” he said in Vandalia, Ohio, “we’re going to win and we’re going to win big. And we’re going to shove it up their ass, OK?”

He depicts himself as all-powerful. “I can do whatever I want,” he told reporters in the Oval Office recently. As if to prove it, he regularly tries to rename bodies of water after America or himself. He demanded that tech companies stop using the term artificial intelligence, preferring instead “super intelligence”; those that disobey, he wrote online, are “THE ENEMY!”

He has never been burdened with excessive self-awareness, but even so, some of his recent comments have been jarring. The man who dispenses disparaging nicknames like “Talafreako” for James Talarico and “Annie Trannie” for Dr. Annie Andrews insisted with a straight face the other day that “I don’t go around mocking people.”

Likewise, the commander in chief who recently threatened to “annihilate” Iran complained bitterly that he did not win the Nobel Peace Prize. Even so, one night last month he could not remember the name of the prize he covets. “Does anybody know the name of that peace prize?” he asked in Pendleton, then came up with another: “the Pulitzer Prize.”

When he summoned the name of the Nobel Prize last week in Port Huron, Mich., he declared that he would like to ban all immigrants from Norway, where the award committee is based, because he did not win. “I don’t want anybody from Norway,” he said. “Frankly, Norway sucks. Norway has become a shithouse country, actually.”

These days, even Mr. Trump seems aware that eyes are on him, watching and waiting. “I love the weave,” he told the midterm Republican convention in Dallas in September. “You know what the weave is? You talk about something, then you bring in a ballroom or you bring in an airplane or you bring in Air Force One. But you notice I always get right back to the same topic.”

And yet, he went on, “when someday, there’ll be a time when I do the weave is weave, weave. Someday, there’ll be a time when I don’t get back to the original subject, and then you can say he’s had it. OK? You can say then he’s had it.”

Methodology

The Times collected thousands of Mr. Trump’s speeches, interviews, social media posts and schedules using data from Roll Call’s Factba.se from 2015 through late October this year. To quantify Mr. Trump’s use of all-or-nothing language and swearwords, we measured basic word frequency statistics across Mr. Trump’s presidential terms and campaign periods. To identify confusing and rambling passages of text, we used the A.I. model Claude Opus 5.5 to score more than 6,500 passages of Mr. Trump’s speeches with detailed instructions based on our previous reporting analyzing Mr. Trump’s use of rambling and profane language. We counted a speech passage as incoherent if it scored at least a seven out of 10 with this rubric, which was informed by manual review of hundreds of passages and an evaluation to ensure a high bar of accuracy.

item.title: This Republican Wants Voters to Consider a Post-Trump World
item.description:
Debra Smith arrived at a recent candidates forum hating John E. Sununu, the Republican nominee for Senate in New Hampshire.

Here, she thought, was another career politician — a former congressman and one-term senator seeking to reclaim his seat nearly 20 years after he lost it, riding the coattails of his father and his brother, both former governors of the state.

A funny thing happened, though, as Mr. Sununu took questions about health care, housing and transportation policy from Chamber of Commerce types as they picked at caprese sandwiches. Ms. Smith found herself impressed as Mr. Sununu wove facts and experience into his answers, lifting the energy of the room.

“He’s very substantial,” she said.

But before Mr. Sununu left the function room at the Atlantic Grill in Rye, N.H., Ms. Smith, an independent voter, told him she still couldn’t vote for him.

“Because of Trump, I can’t,” she said. “I told him I can’t take the risk.”

Mr. Sununu, 62, has turned his comeback Senate campaign into a test of a tricky premise: that in 2026, it is possible to be both a Republican and independent of President Trump. Selling this idea is critical for any hope of success in a purple state that has never really warmed to the president. And as he trails Representative Chris Pappas, a Democrat, in the polls, he’s running out of time to convince the Debra Smiths of the world to buy it, particularly in a race that is considered critical to determining the balance of power in the Senate.

He is trying. He once wrote an opinion essay that carried the headline “Trump is a loser.” He has insisted in a television ad that he has never even met the president. He rattles off a laundry list of their policy differences to anyone who will listen. And, perhaps more than any other Republican running for Senate right now, he has asked voters to do something that strains the American political imagination: Consider what happens after Mr. Trump.

“In two years, the president will leave office,” he said on a debate stage last month. “And my question is, where do we go next?”

The unsaid part of his bet is that, deep down, voters want a political future that looks like the past.

New Hampshire Republicans have lost every race for the House and the Senate since the dawn of the Trump era, often by quite a lot, even as they have won office at the state level. But the party saw a ray of hope in the Sununu name, which is synonymous with the flinty, establishment Republicanism that used to be a lot more common in New England. Mr. Sununu’s father, John H. Sununu, served as governor for three two-year terms in the 1980s before serving as chief of staff to President George H.W. Bush.

National Republicans had tried unsuccessfully to convince Chris Sununu, Mr. Sununu’s charismatic younger brother and a former governor, to run for the Senate in 2022 against the incumbent Democrat, Maggie Hassan. By early 2025, they were seeking to lure John E. Sununu into the 2026 race. But when Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the longtime Democratic incumbent, announced she would retire, Chris Sununu coyly hinted he might run for the Senate after all. A person familiar with the recruiting efforts said that national Republicans checked in to gauge how serious he was — nobody wanted two Sununus on the ballot, after all — but Chris ultimately demurred.

Today, the campaign signs dotting the state’s landscape read, simply, “Sununu Senator,” without specifying which one is actually running. Democrats have conducted private polling to see if voters know which family member is on the ballot. They say confusion abounds.

One reporter’s text message meant for John E. Sununu recently made it, instead, to his father.

“You have reached the old ancient former Gov. of New Hampshire,” came the reply, which concluded, “not the young dynamic Sen.”

The current candidate says there is no confusion. “Voters absolutely know who I am,” he said.

Mr. Sununu first ran for Congress 30 years ago and held the seat currently occupied by Mr. Pappas for three terms. He won his Senate seat in 2002, in a strong year for Republicans in the wake of Sept. 11, and lost it to Ms. Shaheen in the wave that accompanied the election of Barack Obama in 2008. (He then pursued a lucrative career working at a lobbying firm and sitting on corporate boards.)

On the campaign trail, he tells war stories from another era. He can be trusted to stand up to Mr. Trump, he says, because he stood up to President George W. Bush, insisting that the reauthorization of the Patriot Act, passed after the Sept. 11 attacks, include more protections for civil liberties. He can be trusted to be bipartisan, he says, because he cosponsored legislation with Hillary Clinton. He was the first Republican to call for the firing of Alberto Gonzales, the attorney general for Mr. Bush. (Mr. Gonzales resigned in 2007 after a standoff with congressional critics over the Justice Department’s handling of terrorism investigations and the firing of U.S. attorneys.)

“I think all of those things reinforce a reputation for independence and for directness and honesty,” he said in an interview.

And did his family name help?

“Sure,” he said, quickly changing the subject to how, in 2024, he endorsed former Gov. Nikki Haley of South Carolina for president over Mr. Trump.

In February, Mr. Trump endorsed Mr. Sununu, saying he would work “tirelessly to advance our America first agenda.”

It was a signal to the party to ignore Mr. Sununu’s primary opponent, another former Republican senator named Scott Brown. But it gave Mr. Pappas his biggest attack line: that, for all his claims of independence, Mr. Sununu is as beholden to Mr. Trump as anyone in a Republican Party that has shown total fealty to the president. Mr. Pappas has also depicted him as squishy on Mr. Trump, saying that Mr. Sununu’s opposition to the war in Iran, for instance, has bloomed only alongside its unpopularity.

Mr. Sununu has tried to keep his focus on his state.

“My focus has been on New Hampshire, on the economy, jobs, affordability, and that message has resonated, and that’s why this is a race that a year ago people didn’t think would be competitive,” Mr. Sununu said.

A New York Times/Siena University poll released in late September found Mr. Pappas with a five-point lead — a sign that Mr. Sununu is running significantly more competitively than the state’s last two Republican Senate nominees. One of them, Corky Messner, lost to Ms. Shaheen by nearly 16 percentage points in 2020; the other, Don Bolduc, lost to Senator Maggie Hassan by 9 points. (In a twist, Mr. Bolduc has endorsed Mr. Pappas.)

In that poll, Mr. Sununu’s favorability rating was slightly higher than Mr. Pappas’s, at 45 percent to 43 percent. And 48 percent of voters said Mr. Sununu would better handle issues related to the cost of living; 46 percent said that about Mr. Pappas.

But 60 percent of voters disapproved of Mr. Trump, and 54 percent said they wanted a candidate who would provide a check on him.

As he spoke to the Seacoast Chamber Alliance late last month, Mr. Sununu seemed, at times, to be inhabiting a kind of Brigadoon where there was no President Trump.

He called for term limits in Congress, lamented the unbalanced state of the federal budget and eagerly parried questions about Social Security, going deep into the weeds.

Mr. Pappas had addressed the group first. When he finished, Jimmy Dykes, an independent voter from the coastal town of Hampton, asked why the congressman had not been more visible in that community. But Mr. Dykes said he was planning to vote for Mr. Pappas, anyway.

He associated Mr. Sununu with the wars that began during his tenure in Congress, those in Iraq and Afghanistan, and said he simply couldn’t trust him to deal with Mr. Trump, who he believes is an “existential threat.”

Mr. Dykes was, however, considering voting for Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican who has also stayed well away from Mr. Trump. She used to have the job Mr. Sununu wants but narrowly lost re-election to the Senate the night Mr. Trump was elected in 2016. Now, she appears to be cruising to re-election as governor — becoming one of her party’s bright spots in a difficult year.

Mr. Sununu, for his part, declined to say what he thought the Republican Party should look like after Mr. Trump is gone. But does he want to help shape it?

“Absolutely.”

Bayliss Wagner contributed reporting.

item.title: Culture War Tensions Roil Beverly Hills School Board Race
item.description:
Since the Covid-19 pandemic, school board elections around the country, once sleepy affairs, have been convulsed by America’s political and cultural divides. The teaching of racial justice. Gaza and Israel. Transgender rights.

But very few of these battles have had the same mix of wealth, privilege and celebrity as the one that is going on in Beverly Hills, Calif. And this year, the campaign for two seats on the school board has devolved into an all-out political brawl.

“The ugliness of national politics has come to Beverly Hills,” said Gay Abrams, 70, an activist who has lived in the city for decades and recently organized “No Kings” rallies.

Moles have infiltrated group chats. The police have responded to dozens of calls about stolen campaign signs. One of the candidates has a restraining order against an opponent over allegations of doxxing. And in this heavily Jewish community, feelings about Israel and the definition of antisemitism have been at the forefront.

Beverly Hills, while it has always had plenty of Republicans, for decades voted for Democrats for president, save for Ronald Reagan. That changed in 2024, when the city, which has a population of about 30,000, voted for Donald Trump and became a small red dot on the vast blue map of Los Angeles County.

That same year, two new school board members were elected in Beverly Hills, securing a narrow 3-2 conservative majority.

And then controversies began piling up, starting with a pro-Trump rally at Beverly Hills High School after the 2024 election. Minority students said they were bullied, with pro-Trump students yelling, “Deport all Mexicans,” according to a lawsuit filed by a teacher who said she had been fired for a social media post criticizing the rally.

Over time, tensions boiled over arcane issues like when to allow public comment at board meetings and how the bylaws say the board’s vice president should be elected. Then came the political disputes: whether to display the Israeli flag at schools; the inclusion of Charlie Kirk next to notable Americans such as Martin Luther King Jr. at an elementary school exhibit; and the removal of a Maya Angelou book from the same exhibit.

The school board race is nonpartisan, but the rift involves familiar divisions. The conservative board majority has been supportive of Israel and resistant to recognizing ethnic history. Liberals have pushed for celebrating more diversity and said that criticism of Israel does not equate to antisemitism.

On the conservative side of the school board race is Judy Manouchehri, 46, a lawyer and the incumbent president, as well as an ally, David Cienfuegos, 53, a personal injury attorney who grew up in Mexico and California. On the liberal side are two political newcomers: Jackie Kruger, a 47-year-old lawyer and mother; and Kim Lifschitz, 39, a stay-at-home mother.

The four candidates, along with a fifth entrant who has less traction, are competing for two at-large seats that all voters in the school district will choose.

Ms. Manouchehri, who grew up in Beverly Hills after her family fled Iran following the revolution in 1979, considers herself nonpartisan and said she would prefer to focus on the district’s improvements in test scores. (While some data shows gains in test scores, her opponents have pointed to a decline in Beverly Hills High School’s ranking in the U.S. News & World Report.)

She said she was frustrated by the divisiveness within the Beverly Hills Unified School District.

“It’s something that hurts and is disappointing, and I wake up every day and one of my goals is to try to counter the negativity with facts, data and reasons for the Beverly Hills community to be proud of B.H.U.S.D.,” she said in a recent interview.

She said dust-ups over culture war issues are rare, and exaggerated on social media. Still, she apologized for two episodes that have fueled divisions in the city.

In one, she voted against a resolution establishing cultural heritage months, including Black History Month, asking why the city didn’t celebrate a European heritage month. “Looking back, I don’t think I realized the gravity it held for the community,” she said. (The resolution passed on a 3-to-2 vote.)

“I do regret the hurt that my vote on that resolution caused,” she added.

In another, she said it was a mistake for a school club to host the Israeli American influencer Ben Azoulay, who once served jail time after pleading guilty to a sex crime with a minor. She said Mr. Azoulay slipped through the district’s vetting process.

The controversy over Mr. Azoulay was one of the reasons Ms. Kruger decided to run for school board. The incumbents, she said, are “creating chaos and sowing division and demonstrating that they are only here to serve a very small minority.”

Ms. Kruger fled the Soviet Union in 1980, and she said her parents had sacrificed so she could attend Beverly Hills schools.

On a recent evening, residents supporting her and Ms. Lifschitz packed into her modest white cottage on a tree-lined street of multimillion-dollar homes that pass for a middle-class enclave in Beverly Hills and feel far away from the wide lawns and estates on the other side of town.

Over sandwiches and plates of kebab, parents worked the phones, dialing voters.

Ms. Kruger had spent much of the day in court, for a hearing about continuing the restraining order she had secured against Mr. Cienfuegos, whom she has accused of videotaping her home, posting her address on social media and accusing her son of stealing campaign signs.

“This is our opportunity, overnight, to come back to normalcy,” she said of the board election.

Ms. Lifschitz, 39, said she had decided to run to counter what she saw as an extreme, rightward shift of the district.

“It’s really scary to me to see this, honestly, this MAGA infiltration down to this local level,” she said.

During the campaign, Ms. Lifschitz became engulfed in controversy when, in group chats, she appeared to mock both a picture of one school board member at the Western Wall in Jerusalem and the way another board member introduced Holocaust survivors at an event in a “sing-song-y voice like they were pets in a zoo.” Screenshots were leaked online, and Ms. Lifschitz, who is Jewish, was accused of being an antisemite. (“It was just adults venting,” she said.)

Talk to residents long enough about the political upheaval in their city, and they will point to a deeper clash that goes back decades, when Persians, many of them Jews, fled the Iranian Revolution and settled in Beverly Hills. Persian Jews tend to be more conservative — many support the war on Iran, for example — than the old guard of Beverly Hills, who are predominantly Ashkenazi Jews of European descent.

Many liberal Jews in Beverly Hills believe the school board has focused too much on Israel and point to an effort to have schools display the Israeli flag. (After an uproar, the superintendent backed down, citing safety concerns.)

“I’m Jewish and I was raised in this district and I don’t really want my board focusing on a foreign country and an issue that has nothing to do with my classroom,” said Amy Arebalo, who taught in the district for decades and retired last year. “But this has become the board’s priority.”

On a recent afternoon, Russell Stuart, a conservative incumbent not facing re-election, was at his desk at Beverly Hills Guns, an appointment-only gun dealer located on the fifth floor of an office building on Wilshire Boulevard. Mr. Stuart runs a website, the Beverly Hills Standard, that produces articles generated by artificial intelligence that have attacked his opponents.

He framed the split in Beverly Hills as one largely within the Jewish community. The entire five-member school board, including Mr. Stuart, is Jewish.

“I think that in the city of Beverly Hills there’s definitely a divide between the white Jews and the Persian Jews,” said Mr. Stuart.

“It’s absolutely undeniable how well the Persians have done, in this country and this state and this city,” he added. “And I think that there is a resentment, truly a resentment of how well they’ve done.”

Asked about this divide, Ms. Manouchehri said, “It’s starting to feel that way.”

Across the political divide of Beverly Hills, there is a sense of loss — of the civility and decorum people say once defined public life in the city.

“Everyone is just, it’s sad and tiresome,” said David Lucky, 48, a television producer who has a daughter in third grade.

“I don’t know why,” he continued. “I don’t think anyone knows why. And I don’t know what happens after.”

item.title: A Midterm Campaign Dominated by Concerns Over High Prices Nears Its End
item.description:
Financial concerns have been the most pressing issue for voters in four of the six previous midterm elections of this century. But with the war in Iran and tariffs driving up gas prices, inflation and mortgage rates, the worries feel deeper, more desperate and decidedly center stage in the final days of the hard-fought campaign that will decide control of Congress.

Democrats are hammering President Trump for starting a war with Iran and instituting tariffs that have driven up prices, while Republicans are insisting the fundamentals of the economy are stronger than before they took power two years ago. And polls show that pocketbook issues are once again top of mind for many voters.

If presidential elections are about a vision for the future, midterms give voters a chance to offer their verdict on a president, a Congress and, almost always, the nation’s economic health.

Over dozens of interviews across the country in recent days, Americans from across the political spectrum detailed the financial gymnastics of keeping pace with rent hikes and mounting utility bills, along with rising prices for gas, groceries and even Halloween candy. Many voters directly blamed Mr. Trump and his party for the high cost of living.

“The prices of everything we normally buy have gone up and up dramatically,” said Dwayne Stanford, a father of eight in suburban Cincinnati, who chose only Democratic candidates during early voting in his state. “It’s just the everyday stuff.”

“Everybody’s feeling it in terms of inflation,” said Bret Rhodus, 52, an independent voter from Douglas County, Kan. “College costs, because I’m kind of in that stage of life. But even, like, the price of a pizza.”

“It’s expensive,” said Sophia Gallerani, 80, a retiree who said she cast her ballot for the Republican ticket on the first day of early voting in Tucson, Ariz. “Basic needs like eating and gas for getting to appointments if I have any or going to church.”

The worries of voters, which cross lines of generation and gender, race and political ideology, reflect the anxieties of a country convinced that the American dream is slipping away. In polls, focus groups and interviews, voters described some of the traditional promises of a middle-class life — health care, a college education, homeownership and retirement — as becoming rapidly unaffordable. They fear their children will live a worse life than they do.

“I have a degree, I have a good job, but it is still a stretch to pay for basics like groceries and utilities,” said Brandi Kelly, 43, of Dayton, Ohio. “It is harder to just maintain what we have had.”

Presidents often shoulder the blame — and occasionally the credit — for an American economy that they have limited ability to directly control. But Douglas Holtz-Eakin, the former chief economist for President George W. Bush’s Council of Economic Advisers and current president of the conservative American Action Forum, said that old political maxim doesn’t totally apply when it comes to Mr. Trump and some of the signature policies of his administration.

The war with Iran raised gas prices, and tariffs made foreign goods more expensive for U.S. purchasers. The rising costs have outpaced workers’ hourly wages, according to the government, compounding the financial stress already felt by many American families.

“The standard of living is declining and people know that,” Mr. Holtz-Eakin said. “The nature of these actions have really allowed voters to blame him.”

Democrats have driven a message of blaming Mr. Trump for the high costs. Expanding on a theme of “affordability” that the party rode to success in the races for governor in 2025, Democratic candidates and their allies have spent nearly a half-billion dollars on ads mentioning the economy, prices and inflation, according to AdImpact.

In Maine, Troy Jackson, the Democratic Senate nominee, has transformed surging heating oil costs into a central line of attack against Senator Susan Collins, the Republican incumbent.

In North Carolina, former Gov. Roy Cooper, the Democratic Senate nominee, has spent weeks on a “Make Stuff Cost Less” campaign tour, introducing plans to lower the price of food, health care, utilities, child care and housing.

And in Texas, supporters of Gina Hinojosa, the Democratic nominee for governor, wave money-green signs with one of her central campaign promises: “Money in your pocket.”

Even in races dominated by questions of character and corruption, Democrats have steadfastly returned to high costs as the central building block of their political argument.

“We can’t afford the basics in this economy — gas, groceries, utilities, health care — because the system has been rigged by billionaires and crooked politicians like Ken Paxton,” James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas, told a cheering crowd at the Kay Bailey Hutchison Convention Center in Dallas on Thursday evening, referring to his Republican opponent. “This election is about whether you want a senator who puts money in your pocket or money in their own.”

As he crisscrosses the country on a whirlwind campaign tour, Mr. Trump has tried to argue that the economy is strong, growing and rife with new investment. Markets are riding high, consumers are continuing to spend and gross domestic product is increasing, according to recent measures.

But as Mr. Trump’s predecessor, former President Joseph R. Biden Jr., learned during his term in office, voters don’t care how government reports assess the economy. They care how it feels.

“The problem is that the one metric people use to judge the economy is gas prices,” said Steve Moore, a conservative economist who advised Mr. Trump’s first presidential campaign. “You see it wherever you go, with a big sign.”

Some of Mr. Trump’s most devoted supporters continue to profess their loyalty, even as they describe enduring economic pain.

Brenda Pruitt, a three-time voter for Mr. Trump, said she had spent more than $100 on gasoline to drive to Ohio from Kentucky to see the president and other Republican candidates speak at a rally in Chillicothe, Ohio, on Wednesday,

“I’m feeling the inflation, but I’m willing to take less in order to help the American people,” Ms. Pruitt said.

At the rally, Mr. Trump touted the performance of the stock market and higher incomes while blaming Democrats for voting for policies that led to higher prices.

“They voted in favor of the worst inflation and highest energy costs in American history,” Mr. Trump said.

That’s an argument Mr. Trump spent much of 2024 making. More than any other issue, his rise into the White House was fueled by attacks on Mr. Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris for high inflation and promises to lower soaring prices.

Two years later, with inflation rising once again, large numbers of voters have shifted blame to Mr. Trump. Views of his handling of the economy — one of his biggest strengths when he ran on two years ago — are now underwater. Majorities disapprove of his handling of tariffs, the economy, gas prices, the cost of living and the Iran war. Fifty-three percent of likely voters considered the economy as “poor,” in the recent New York Times/Siena poll — the worst rating since July 2022.

Mr. Trump promised to lower inflation; it’s now accelerated to 3.7 percent. He vowed mortgage rates would return to as low as 2 percent. They are currently above 7 percent. And surging fuel prices have increased the costs for farmers, truckers and consumers to heat their homes, plow their fields and commute to work.

Republican efforts to defend the president’s policies, despite growing anger from voters, have fueled Democratic optimism in some surprising places. A clip posted in February of Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican from Mississippi, responding to concerns about rising beef prices by saying consumers “have so many proteins to choose from,” helped transform her race in a deep red state into a competitive contest.

Her opponent, Scott Colom, has gained ground with a simple slogan: “High wages, lower costs, save our health care.”

In Kansas, Senator Roger Marshall, a Republican, was slow to respond to the rising costs of fertilizer, fuel and feed that have hammered farmers and ranchers in his agriculture-heavy state. The race, which was not on either party’s list of battleground states last year, is now considered one of the most competitive in the country.

“This is one of the best economies I’ve ever seen in my lifetime,” Mr. Marshall said at a campaign stop last month. “We just have to get the price of gas and groceries down.”

The White House has tried to find ways to offer consumers some relief, announcing a series of policies in the final weeks of the campaign that included $90 payouts for millions of seniors on Medicare, $500 rebate checks for some Affordable Care Act customers and a decision to allow Russian diesel imports after years of sanctions.

Mr. Trump has also promised a $5,000 check to every American adult if his party retains control of Congress in November. The plan would require congressional approval and cost more than $1 trillion.

But for many people, such policies are coming too late to affect their finances — or their votes.

As Carmen Moreno, 50, waited to hear Mr. Talarico address the crowd in Dallas, she expressed astonishment at the increase in the cost of food. A recent trip to Denny’s with her mother cost $63, she said.

Ms. Moreno, an entrepreneur, is hopeful Mr. Talarico and a Democratic-controlled Congress can help restore an American middle class that she worries is slipping away.

“We are living in a time with a lot of economic distress,” she said. “And there’s just a total lack of accountably in Congress right now. Like, what is going on?”

Kevin Williams contributed reporting from Butler County, Ohio, Ilana Arougheti from Douglas County, Kan., and Lourdes Medrano from Tucson, Ariz.
